blocks.text: A patient with migraine brings three things to clinic about a herbal supplement: a glowing testimonial from a friend, a magazine article describing 12 patients who improved, and a printout of a systematic review. All three are 'evidence', but they differ enormously in how much they can mislead you. The hierarchy of evidence is a way of ranking that vulnerability.

blocks.markdown: Evidence does not all carry equal weight. Study designs differ in how well they protect against **bias**, a systematic error that pushes results away from the truth. The better a design controls the two main threats, **confounding** (a third factor related to both exposure and outcome) and **selection and measurement bias**, the higher it sits in the hierarchy *for a question about treatment effects*. Different questions need different designs, so the hierarchy is a guide, not a law.

rows: Depends on quality of included trials and completeness of search; publication bias
Poor concealment, lack of blinding, attrition
Recall and selection bias, confounding, cannot give incidence
No comparison group; selective reporting of striking cases
Unsystematic experience, authority and belief; no control of bias
blocks.caption: A typical hierarchy for questions about the effects of treatment. Observational designs can be the best available for harms, prognosis and rare outcomes.

blocks.title: Confounding and bias
blocks.text: **Confounding** occurs when an unmeasured or uncontrolled factor distorts the apparent relationship between an exposure and an outcome, for example people who take supplements may also exercise more. **Bias** is any systematic departure from the true effect. Randomisation distributes known and unknown confounders evenly on average, which is why randomised trials rank above observational studies for treatment effects; it does not remove the need to check conduct and analysis.

blocks.title: Ranking five sources about a herbal supplement for migraine
blocks.prompt: Rank the following by susceptibility to bias and name the main weakness of each: (1) a friend's testimonial, (2) a case series of 12 patients who improved, (3) a cohort study of supplement users and non-users, (4) a randomised controlled trial of 200 patients with blinding, (5) a systematic review of several such trials.

steps.text: The testimonial is one unsystematic account without a comparison, subject to recall, placebo response and the natural fluctuation of migraine, so it is most susceptible to bias.
The case series has no control group and reports only selected patients, so improvement may reflect natural history or regression to the mean.
The cohort study compares groups, but users and non-users may differ in other ways (confounding), so associations may not be causal.
The randomised, blinded trial controls confounding and bias in conduct, but one trial may be imprecise or unrepresentative.
The systematic review of trials combines multiple trials through a reproducible, appraised method, giving the most reliable estimate if the search is complete and the trials are sound.

blocks.answer: Least to most reliable: testimonial, case series, cohort study, RCT, systematic review of RCTs. The ranking presumes each is well conducted.

blocks.markdown: **Primary studies, systematic reviews and guidelines.** A **primary study** collects new data from participants (trial, cohort, case-control, cross-sectional). A **systematic review** is a secondary study with a pre-specified, reproducible method for searching, selecting, appraising and synthesising primary studies; a **meta-analysis** statistically combines their results. A narrative (traditional) review summarises evidence without that method and is vulnerable to selective citation. A **guideline** is a different kind of document: it uses systematic evidence together with judgements on harms, costs, values and feasibility to make *recommendations for practice*, often graded by strength of evidence (for example NICE guidance, which uses systematic reviews and GRADE-based certainty ratings).

rows: Answer a question with new data
One sample; may be biased or imprecise
Answer a focused question from all relevant studies
Garbage in, garbage out; publication bias
Panel values and conflicts of interest; may lag behind new evidence
blocks.caption: Distinguishing the three main levels of evidence sources. Pre-appraised sources (reviews and guidelines) save time but should still be checked for date and rigour.

blocks.markdown: **Publication bias.** Studies with positive or statistically significant results are more likely to be submitted, accepted and published, so the visible literature overstates benefit. Related problems are **outcome reporting bias** (only favourable outcomes reported), language bias and delayed publication. Remedies: prospective trial registration, publication of protocols and results regardless of outcome, searching registries and grey literature, and examining a **funnel plot** of effect size against precision: in the absence of bias small studies scatter symmetrically around the pooled effect, while a gap where small negative studies should be suggests missing studies (though other causes of asymmetry exist).

blocks.title: How selective publication distorts the literature
blocks.prompt: Twenty trials of a drug are registered. In truth 8 show benefit (positive) and 12 do not. All 8 positive trials are published, but only 4 of the 12 neutral or negative trials are published. What proportion of published trials are positive, compared with the true proportion?

steps.text: The true proportion positive among all registered trials.
Proportion positive among the published trials.

Selective publication raises the apparent proportion of positive trials from 40% to 67%, so a review that searched only journals would conclude the drug works more often than it truly does, and a pooled effect would be inflated.

blocks.answer: The published literature shows 67% positive trials versus 40% in truth: an inflation of about 27 percentage points caused by publication bias.

blocks.title: Predatory journals
blocks.text: **Predatory (or deceptive) journals** charge publication fees but provide little or no genuine peer review or editorial service, often with misleading claims about indexing or impact factors. Because they publish almost anything, their content may be unreliable and pollute searches and citations. Warning signs: unsolicited emails flattering the author, promises of very rapid acceptance, vague or hidden fees, unclear editorial board or contact details, misleading metrics, and a scope covering everything. Check that the journal is listed in the Directory of Open Access Journals, follows COPE principles, is indexed in a trusted database, and consider the 'Think. Check. Submit.' checklist.

blocks.title: Hierarchy is a starting point
blocks.text: A poorly conducted randomised trial can be worse evidence than a well-conducted cohort study, and a systematic review of biased studies is still biased. For harms that are rare or delayed, observational designs may be the best evidence available. Always appraise the conduct of the study, not only its label.

points: Study designs are ranked by susceptibility to bias and confounding: systematic reviews of RCTs, RCTs, cohort, case-control, case series, then opinion, for questions about treatment.
A primary study collects new data; a systematic review uses a reproducible method to synthesise primary studies; a guideline adds judgement on values and resources to make recommendations.
Publication bias favours positive results and inflates apparent benefit; registration, searching registries and funnel plots help detect it.
Predatory journals provide little real peer review; check indexing, editorial transparency and fees before trusting or submitting.

questions.stem: For a question about whether a treatment works, which of the following sources is generally most susceptible to bias?

options.text: A well-conducted prospective cohort study
A randomised controlled trial with concealed allocation
A description of a single patient who improved after treatment, with no comparison group
A systematic review of randomised trials

questions.correctOptionText: A description of a single patient who improved after treatment, with no comparison group

distractorRationale.a: It has a comparison group and measured data, though confounding remains possible.
distractorRationale.b: Randomisation with concealment protects against selection bias and confounding.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: no comparison group, selective reporting and natural recovery make it highly vulnerable.
distractorRationale.d: It combines multiple trials with a reproducible method.

questions.explanation: Without a comparison group one cannot tell whether improvement is due to the treatment, to the natural history of the illness, regression to the mean or placebo effects. Controlled designs with random allocation, and syntheses of them, are much less susceptible to such bias.

questions.stem: A large cohort study finds that people who regularly take a nutritional supplement have fewer heart attacks than non-users. Why is this weaker evidence of benefit than a randomised trial?

options.text: Cohort studies cannot measure heart attacks
A larger sample always increases bias
Observational studies are never published in journals
Supplement users may differ in other health-related behaviours, so confounding could explain the difference

questions.correctOptionText: Supplement users may differ in other health-related behaviours, so confounding could explain the difference

distractorRationale.a: Cohort studies can measure outcomes; confounding is the problem.
distractorRationale.b: Sample size reduces random error, not systematic error.
distractorRationale.c: Observational studies are regularly published; their weakness is design, not publication.
distractorRationale.d: Correct: without randomisation, groups may differ in diet, exercise and other factors.

questions.explanation: Healthy-user effects and other confounders can create or exaggerate an association that is not causal. Randomisation balances known and unknown confounders on average, which is why it ranks higher for questions about treatment effects.

questions.stem: Which feature best distinguishes a systematic review from a narrative review?

options.text: The use of a longer reference list
A pre-specified, reproducible method for searching, selecting and appraising studies
Publication in a high-impact journal
The reviewer being an expert in the field

questions.correctOptionText: A pre-specified, reproducible method for searching, selecting and appraising studies

distractorRationale.a: Length does not make a review systematic.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: systematic methods reduce selective citation and allow others to repeat the review.
distractorRationale.c: The venue does not define the method.
distractorRationale.d: Expertise does not replace a reproducible method.

questions.explanation: A systematic review states its question, search strategy, eligibility criteria and appraisal methods in advance, so that its results can be checked and reproduced. A narrative review relies on the author's selection and is therefore more exposed to bias.

questions.stem: An expert panel reads systematic reviews on stroke prevention, considers harms, costs and patient preferences, and publishes graded recommendations for clinicians. How is this document best described?

options.text: A case series
A meta-analysis
A clinical guideline
A primary study

distractorRationale.a: A case series describes a group of patients, not recommendations.
distractorRationale.b: A meta-analysis statistically pools effect estimates; it does not make graded practice recommendations.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: it uses evidence together with judgements to recommend practice.
distractorRationale.d: A primary study collects new data from participants.

questions.explanation: Guidelines draw on systematic reviews but also incorporate values, resource use and feasibility, resulting in recommendations. Their quality depends on the rigour of the review and the transparency of the panel, including management of conflicts of interest.

questions.stem: A systematic review of poorly conducted trials gives high-quality evidence simply because it is a systematic review.

options.text: True
False

questions.explanation: A systematic review can be no better than the studies it includes, so a review of biased trials may still give biased results. Reviewers therefore appraise the risk of bias in included studies and consider the certainty of the evidence.

questions.stem: In a meta-analysis, the funnel plot shows many small studies with large benefits but a conspicuous absence of small studies with null or harmful results. What does this suggest?

options.text: The trials had perfect allocation concealment
Possible publication bias, with small negative studies missing from the literature
The pooled effect is certainly unbiased
The included trials had no heterogeneity

questions.correctOptionText: Possible publication bias, with small negative studies missing from the literature

distractorRationale.a: Allocation concealment cannot be inferred from a funnel plot.
distractorRationale.b: Correct: asymmetry suggests small studies with unfavourable results may not have been published.
distractorRationale.c: The asymmetry raises concern about bias; it does not support unbiasedness.
distractorRationale.d: Funnel asymmetry is not a measure of heterogeneity.

questions.explanation: Small studies are more variable, so they should scatter on both sides of the pooled effect. If one side is empty, small studies with negative results may be unpublished, although other causes, such as heterogeneity, can also produce asymmetry.

questions.stem: A junior doctor receives an email inviting them to submit a manuscript to an unfamiliar journal, promising acceptance within 3 days and quoting a fee only after acceptance. What is the best response?

options.text: Accept because the journal contacted them personally, which proves it is reputable
Pay the fee first to confirm the journal is genuine
Treat it as a possible predatory journal, check indexing, editorial board and fee transparency, and be prepared to decline
Submit immediately because rapid publication helps a career

questions.correctOptionText: Treat it as a possible predatory journal, check indexing, editorial board and fee transparency, and be prepared to decline

distractorRationale.a: Unsolicited flattery is a typical tactic of deceptive journals.
distractorRationale.b: Payment does not verify legitimacy and should not precede checking.
distractorRationale.c: Correct: rapid guaranteed acceptance and hidden fees are typical warning signs.
distractorRationale.d: Publishing in a predatory outlet can damage credibility and the work may not be properly reviewed.

questions.explanation: Predatory journals offer little real peer review and often hide fees or exaggerate indexing. Checking the Directory of Open Access Journals, COPE membership, indexing in trusted databases and the transparency of the editorial process protects both the author and the integrity of the literature.

questions.stem: Thirty trials of a drug are registered. In truth 12 show benefit and 18 show no benefit. All 12 positive trials are published, but only 6 of the 18 non-positive trials are published. By how many percentage points does the published literature overstate the proportion of positive trials?
questions.explanation: The true proportion positive is $12/30=40\%$. Published trials number $12+6=18$, of which 12 are positive, so the published proportion is $12/18=66.7\%$. The overstatement is $66.7-40.0=26.7$ percentage points, showing how selective publication distorts the literature a clinician sees.

questions.stem: Explain what is meant by a hierarchy of evidence for therapy questions. Place the following in order from most to least susceptible to bias and say why: case report, RCT, cohort study, systematic review of RCTs. Explain also two limitations of using the hierarchy mechanically.
markingGuide: Hierarchy ranks designs by their protection against bias and confounding for treatment effect questions
Order (least reliable to most): case report, cohort study, RCT, systematic review of RCTs
Case report: no comparison group; cohort: comparison but confounding; RCT: randomisation controls confounding; systematic review: combines trials with a reproducible method
Limitation: a poorly conducted RCT can be worse than a good cohort study; design label does not replace appraisal
Limitation: different questions need different designs (harms, prognosis, diagnosis, rare outcomes)
Systematic reviews depend on included studies and completeness of search
questions.explanation: A hierarchy captures how well each design controls bias for treatment questions, from uncontrolled reports through observational to randomised designs and their syntheses. It must be combined with critical appraisal because execution and the type of question can override the nominal rank.

questions.stem: Describe publication bias, explain how it can distort a systematic review, and describe how a reviewer detects and reduces it. Then give three features of a predatory journal.
markingGuide: Publication bias: studies with positive or significant results are more likely to be published
Distortion: review of published studies overestimates benefit and underestimates harm
Detection: funnel plot asymmetry, comparison of registry entries with publications
Reduction: prospective trial registration, searching registries and grey literature, contacting authors, publishing regardless of result
Predatory journal features: unsolicited invitations, very rapid acceptance with little genuine peer review, hidden fees, misleading indexing or metrics
Check DOAJ, COPE and trusted indexing before relying on or submitting to a journal
questions.explanation: Selective publication distorts the evidence base by hiding unfavourable studies, so pooled effects appear larger than they are. Reviewers counter it with comprehensive searching including registries, funnel plots and comparison of protocols with reports, while authors and readers must also be alert to predatory journals that lack genuine editorial standards.
